model:llama|title:introducing the llama.content_excerpt: The llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware. Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance. You can choose Hardware , Model , and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201). Both tests start at context depth zero ( n_depth=0 ). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput ( avg_ts ). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows. We benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh , the build and installation project behind llama.app . The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration. The model set evolves and currently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M , Q8_0 , other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16 . The explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model. Standard results use <build>/<hardware>/<model>/<quant>.jsonl . Workload sweeps use the same folder <quant>-tg.jsonl filename. Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run. Thanks to the AMD team for providing test infrastructure and helping validate the setup! Try the dashboard , inspect the data , and let us know which models and workloads you would like to see next.

model:nemotron|ver:3.5|title:building on.content_excerpt: We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse , a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents. Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference . We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion. Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications. Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation. This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process. Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples : rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values. Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples : rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships. OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples : synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading. Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language. We trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. story|title:agent security shouldn t be.content_excerpt: What agentic AI security means, the OWASP Top 10 risks for AI agents, and a step-by-step way to secure agents with permissions, approvals, limits and records. Agentic AI security is the work of protecting AI agents, the tools they can use and the systems they reach, so that an agent can only take the actions it was meant to take, even when it reads bad information or a hidden malicious instruction. You cannot make the model itself fully trustworthy. Secure the agent around it instead: limit what it can reach, enforce its permissions outside the model, hold consequential actions for a person, cap how much it can do in one run, and record everything it does. Then assume something will get through and make sure the damage stays small. A chatbot gives an answer that a person can ignore. An agent takes actions. It reads email, opens web pages, calls APIs, updates records, sends messages and sometimes runs code, often with real credentials and without anyone watching each step. That changes the attack surface. Every email, document, web page, tool result and message from another agent the agent reads is input that can shape what it does next. OWASP describes prompt injection as user prompts that alter the model's behavior or output in unintended ways, and the same is true of text hidden inside content the agent retrieves. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre puts the core problem plainly: current large language models do not enforce a security boundary between instructions and data inside a prompt. Agent security therefore cannot depend on the model telling the two apart. The OWASP GenAI Security Project released this peer-reviewed list in December 2025 as the 2026 edition. Names are OWASP's; the one-line explanations are our own summaries. OWASP traces most agent damage to excessive agency, and names three root causes: excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy. In other words, the agent had tools it did not need, access broader than its task, or the freedom to act without a check. A simple example: a support agent that reads incoming email and can also send email to any address. A single email with hidden instructions can turn it into a way to send internal information outside the company. The fix is not a better prompt. It is removing the unrestricted send tool, limiting recipients, or holding outgoing messages for a person. This is not theoretical. story|title:amazon says hackers ai agent.content_excerpt: Amazon said AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server. The agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework. The hackers, who provided prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to the Chinese Standard Time zone, gave the agents a list of IP addresses and the goal: “obtain shell access.” In short order, the agents discovered a zero-day in an open source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers. The agents then exploited the vulnerability and gained full control of the system. “These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable,” Amazon said . Cairn is an open source AI problem-solving engine whose first validated domain is autonomous penetration testing. Users give it a task or goal and, optionally, hints for achieving it. A server maintains a shared graph containing facts and hints. A dispatcher reads the graph, schedules tasks, manages containers, and writes the protocol. The dispatcher can then assign each project to a dedicated worker container, each of which runs multiple agents concurrently. Cairn is model-agnostic and can be used on worker back ends, including Claude Code, Codex, and Pi. Researchers from security firm Palo Alto Networks have also observed Cairn being used with GLM 5.2, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and DeepSeek V4 Pro. Although Cairn was built for defenders, the framework is also benefiting offensive hackers. Earlier this month, Palo Alto Networks said hackers used the framework to target organizations in the semiconductor, defense, and civil society sectors. In all, the campaign conducted 25 autonomous operations against at least 19 organizations. At least 10 of the organizations were successfully breached when Cairn agents performed actions that: Palo Alto Networks said the attackers created tasks with a one-line goal, such as: “Obtain substantive high-value access, including but not limited to webshell, SSH, source code, keys, user information, credentials, ideally, to enter the internal network.” Cairn’s default agent instructions explicitly direct workers to carry out various penetration-testing techniques, including vulnerability exploitation, reverse shells, and data exfiltration. story|title:anthropic created a honeypot.content_excerpt: Leather-clad billionaires aren’t the only ones who can be led astray by alleged honeypots . Researchers at Anthropic have developed Siren , a new honeypot test for artificial intelligence agents. The setup puts agents in realistic simulations designed to tempt them into misbehaving. How they respond will help researchers evaluate the likelihood that new models will go rogue when deployed in the real world, as well as the effectiveness of different safety measures. The test lets agents loose inside one of 26 different simulated sandbox environments. Various features of the sandbox are deliberately misconfigured to allow egress, while an enticing file containing things like passwords and apparent routes onto the internet sits just outside the sandbox boundary. The setup then presents tasks that tempt the agent to reach outside the sandbox without giving it explicit permission to do so. Crucially, the sandbox exists inside a second sandbox that’s cut off from the outside world to avoid real-life mishaps . “Models are going to continue getting better, continue finding zero-day vulnerabilities,” says Darya Kaviani, a researcher at Anthropic who specializes in security and helped develop Siren. A zero-day vulnerability is a previously unknown flaw in a piece of software that can be used to pilfer data or gain unauthorized access. Anthropic’s Mythos models are especially skilled at finding zero-day bugs because they lack the guardrails that normally block this kind of potentially malicious activity. Kaviani says we should assume AI models will become increasingly capable of finding and exploiting zero-days or figuring out other ways to break free from their constraints. The question then becomes whether they’ll resist the temptation to do so. AI agents—models that perfect actions autonomously—are becoming increasingly commonplace. They power capable coding agents like Claude Code and Codex , as well as peppy personal assistants like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots . But the rise of helpful agents has been accompanied by some remarkable bad behavior. Agents tested by Anthropic, OpenAI, and others have broken free from sandboxes and even hacked into other companies in an effort to solve challenging problems. Assuming AI models continue to display such ingenuity, Kaviani says it will be crucial to do more than just patch software. “Even as we strengthen our infrastructure, models will be able to also keep up and be able to find vulnerabilities,” Kaviani says. story|title:chainguard s dan lorenc insi.content_excerpt: Show notes: AI models are finding years of hidden bugs in open source, and Chainguard's Dan Lorenc says the only way out is software automation: point your agents at your upgrades before attackers point theirs at your code. Watch all the AI DevCon NYC 2026 talks: Recorded live at AI DevCon NYC 2026, Guy Podjarny sits down with Dan, founder and CEO of Chainguard, to unpack Black October: PHP2Shell, a remote code execution bug in Brotli, and a 10.0 in GitLab that was really hiding in Ruby's regex engine. Dan explains why Chainguard shipped its PHP2Shell fix once attacks appeared in the wild, ahead of the official patch, why most exploitable bugs never get a CVE, and why the Linux kernel now files one for  Transcript (sampled): project does things differently. Some have a process, some don't, some do things in public, some use a portal like Hacker One or something like that to deal with intake of vulnerability reports. So it all really varies. Um but the typical flow is somebody's a researcher is looking at a project, finds a vulnerability inside of it, uh, writes up … you know, everybody with uh in the network stack kind of did a final check. No one was seeing any exploit traffic yet, but POCs were flying around on GitHub, everyone was publishing these, most were fake and bogus, but some looked kind of real. Uh and then very late Tuesday night, um uh Cloudflare, a bunch of the others uh started seeing … Let me kind of uh interpret that a little bit, which is every uh every change to your code is is uh is a vulnerability fix in some compilation or some kind of constellation. So you might rank it with a CV that is like a low severity because you can't quite figure out ease of exploit. But they're basically all logs as vulnerabilities, … overflow. Um, anthropic on the Glasswing uh public disclosure site uh is talking about thousands and thousands that they've found. And you can see that they've actually stopped looking. They stopped trying to find more because they realized the bottleneck was actually getting this stuff fixed. Um it's not actually hard to get this stuff fixed … But you wouldn't do that. You would ask the agent to do every single dot upgrade by itself uh over weeks uh and then come back at the end. Um that's something an agent can do that a person would never do. story|title:evaluating recent model rele.content_excerpt: Earlier this month we released GDPx , a benchmark designed to measure the domains most valuable for frontier intelligence. Most agentic benchmarks only measure a single domain like coding or legal. The few that try to be comprehensive, like GDPVal or Agent’s Last Exam , make the mistake of selecting domains based on percentage of GDP or the O*NET taxonomy. AI’s impact is nowhere near evenly distributed across the economy today, and we expect this trend to intensify in the future. Many tasks already can’t justify paying for Fable 5.2, much less Fable 7. Thus, if your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful. It’s for this reason that GDPx intentionally forgoes industries like government and real estate, and instead covers the following domains: Our methodology is also unique. To ensure all our tasks are truly representative of their respective domains, we partnered with 14 specialized data partners to make 206 tasks. The single most notable thing about GDPx, however, is its difficulty. Whereas other benchmarks will often debut with the top model scoring over 50%, Opus 5.5—the highest-scoring model on release day—scored just 12% on GDPx. This massive headroom is what allows GDPx to discriminate between future model releases, unlike saturated benchmarks such as Terminal Bench 4.0 . SemiAnalysis is hiring for GDPx! If you’re interested in helping cement GDPx v2 as the world’s best benchmark, reach out to gdpx@semianalysis.com. Since launching GDPx on November 1st, both Anthropic and OpenAI have released new frontier models. Google made a dramatic resurgence with the Gemini 4 series, and we’ve seen notable releases from Alibaba and Moonshot as well. The GDPx leaderboard now looks like this: It’s worth emphasizing that certain models like Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers. If we exclude cyber, biology, and alignment, the three domains where safety classifiers sometimes kick in, and switch to partial grading to get more signal from the extremely difficult legal and finance domains (which default to binary grading), we get the following leaderboard instead. We think you can argue either of these is the “correct” GDPx leaderboard. On one hand, safety classifiers truly limit the usefulness of models in domains like cyber and bio. story|title:hush the fastest computer us.content_excerpt: The fastest computer use for AI agents. Drive any desktop app in the background, 178 ms per action. Hush lets any agent see and drive the apps on your computer, in the background, while you keep working. Read a window, click, type, read it again: 178 ms . The next fastest tool takes 653 ms. That's fast enough to win one-minute bullet against a 2200 chess.com bot, to play the third movement of the Moonlight Sonata at full tempo with every note on time, and to run ten agents on ten apps at once on one machine, all without anything coming to the front. On Cua Driver Bench v2 's background tasks, agents on Hush went 15/15 with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and with Claude Haiku 5.5, the user never disturbed once. Sonnet took a median 17.8 s per task. An agent reads a window as a short outline, sends a batch of steps, and gets back only what changed: Steps: click REF|X,Y , double REF , right REF , set REF VALUE , type [REF] TEXT , key COMBO [xN] , menu A > B , pick REF OPTION , select REF , focus REF , scroll REF up|down|left|right [N] , show REF , drag REF|X,Y to REF|X,Y , wait gone REF | REF | text "T" | 500ms [within 10s] , lane , unlane . Any REF can also be the element as its outline line shows it: click button "Save" , type field[2] "Ada" . Hush finds it when the step runs, so an agent can act on a window it never read, and a batch can reach into a sheet that an earlier step opened. Timeline events, one per line: MS down KEY , MS up KEY , MS tap KEY [HOLD] , MS down X,Y , MS move X,Y , MS up X,Y , MS tap X,Y [HOLD] . Hush plays them on a real-time thread, under a millisecond off schedule at the median. That's it. Then ask your agent to do something in an app. Needs macOS 15 or later. Run hush setup again any time to check permissions or update the skill. On Linux the same command installs a static binary for x86_64 or arm64, and hush setup checks the accessibility bus, Xvfb and ffmpeg instead. On Debian or Ubuntu that's sudo apt install xvfb at-spi2-core ffmpeg ; on Fedora, sudo dnf install xorg-x11-server-Xvfb at-spi2-core ffmpeg-free . story|title:phison shows ssd design with.content_excerpt: Forward-looking: A lot of what AI servers do all day involves pulling data from their SSDs so a CPU or GPU can process it. Phison wants some of that processing to happen before the data ever leaves the drive. The controller maker has detailed an SSD design with its own NPU and 64GB of memory, designed to run PyTorch and llama.cpp directly on the drive. The company showed off the design at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) in Chicago this week. Rather than sending entire datasets to the host, the drive scans and processes data in parallel right where it sits. It then sends back only the results that matter. Phison claims this could cut data transfers by 10 to 100 times for suitable workloads. The host CPU would get some breathing room, too. On paper, the drive's memory delivers 130 GB/s of bandwidth. That's more than four times the 28 GB/s that Phison's upcoming PCIe 6.0 controller can deliver to a host. In other words, the drive can read its own data far faster than it can transfer it to the server. The company also says developers won't need specialized programming tools because the drive supports familiar frameworks such as vLLM and OpenVINO. Oddly, the only compute figure Phison shared for the NPU is 36,800 DMIPS. That's a decades-old CPU integer benchmark. As Tom's Hardware points out , the figure likely describes companion CPU cores on the drive rather than its AI processing power. There's no TOPS rating anywhere in the announcement. The drive also has no product name or sampling date yet. Phison hasn't even said what type of memory it uses. In fact, the company says many of the products and features it showcased are still in development. For now, then, this is more of an architecture proposal than something a data center can actually order. Drives that perform computations aren't new, either. Samsung put an FPGA on its SmartSSD back in 2018 and followed up with a second generation in 2022. But TechRadar reported last year that the drive had all but disappeared from Samsung's lineup. The outlet partly blamed the generative AI boom, which created much greater demand for raw storage capacity than for on-drive processing. Samsung's drive also relied on software and IP that customers had to develop themselves. That makes Phison's promise to support the AI tools developers already use a significant difference. It could give the idea a better chance this time around, assuming the NPU turns out to be as capable as Phison claims. TechSpot is a registered trademark a

story|title:swarms flocks gangs how to b.content_excerpt: This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models. That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50. Multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we update when we're dealing with many agents? In this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from. We've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI announced that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem. But swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so. A big swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. Noam Brown estimates that less than 10% of the Navier-Stokes result came from multi-agent cooperation. In Anthropic's vulnerability-finding experiment , coordinated agents found more bugs than independent agents, but also searched mo

story|title:threat modeling azure mcp se.content_excerpt: An engineer opens an Azure incident and asks an AI assistant: "Why is this application slow?" The assistant queries Azure Monitor, reviews Log Analytics results, inspects an App Service configuration, and compares the affected resource with a healthy deployment. The investigation that once required several portal blades, Azure CLI commands, and Kusto queries can now begin in one conversation. Now consider the same assistant connected to an Azure subscription with permission to restart workloads, change network rules, update resources, or read Key Vault secrets. The question is no longer only whether the answer is accurate. It is whether the assistant can expose sensitive Azure data, interpret attacker-controlled telemetry as instructions, select the wrong subscription or resource group, or turn a diagnostic request into a production change. Azure MCP Server makes the connection possible. Azure identity, authorization, governance, and monitoring determine whether the connection is safe. Azure MCP Server connects compatible AI clients to Azure services through tools. Depending on the configuration, an assistant can inspect resources, query Azure Monitor, and invoke other Azure operations. Microsoft’s Azure MCP Server security guidance emphasizes that the server, its credentials, and the tool inputs and outputs all require protection. Each boundary matters. Which Entra identity is used? Which tenant and subscription are selected? What role assignments apply at the management group, subscription, resource group, and resource scopes? Is the operation read-only? Can a result contain a secret? Is a production change subject to approval? An authenticated Azure request is not automatically an appropriate Azure operation. Help an on-call engineer investigate elevated latency for an App Service. The assistant may read approved Azure Monitor metrics, Log Analytics data, and resource configuration in one production resource group. It must not modify resources, retrieve Key Vault secret values, change networking, or access another subscription. This statement defines the intended scope. Record the Azure assets, identity, tools, data classifications, and allowed destinations involved: Then ask four questions: What are we connecting? What could go wrong? Which Azure control reduces the risk? How will we prove the control worked? A common shortcut is to connect an assistant using an engineer's existing Azure session. story|title:why i m bullish on mcp for 2.content_excerpt: MCP went through the full hype cycle in the last 18 months. Early excitement turned into backlash and confusion fast, with context bloat as the main complaint. When Skills arrived, most developers moved to CLIs and progressive disclosure instead. I never believed in that, and that sentiment is now changing. At Linear and Notion , agents now create roughly half of all issues (~2.4M/week) and pages, with Notion reporting 60x MCP traffic growth. At Atlassian , MCP handles over 5M tool calls per workday, and 44% of those users sit outside software teams where CLIs were never an option. At Neon , agent usage over MCP grows 14% week over week, and even Apple now ships local MCP servers for Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. The protocol is healthy and actively improving. The 2026-07-28 spec dropped stateful sessions and added official extensions, and clients are getting smarter about how they use them. Real tasks almost always take more than 1 tool call, e.g. you list open issues, grab details, check errors, and write a summary. With plain tool calling, every step needs another model turn and dumps information into the context. Joining data across 2 MCP servers uses the model's context as memory for intermediate payloads. Code Mode is changing how agents call MCP servers. Instead of putting 50 tool schemas into the prompt and calling 1 tool per turn, the harness gives the model a sandbox and exposes MCP tools as callable functions. It's already becoming the default in OpenCode 2.0, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Pi, and Factory Droid. Code Mode works best when the model knows what a tool returns before writing code. When an MCP server declares outputSchema alongside inputSchema , the client can generate typed stubs upfront and pass back structuredContent directly. The model chains multiple calls in 1 script, filters and joins in memory where compute is cheap, and returns only what matters. Compared to CLIs, MCP servers are natively multimodal. A tool call can return typed structuredContent for code alongside separate image, audio, or embedded resource blocks. Auth is also cleaner. CLIs and raw curl force you to store API keys on disk or in environment variables with broad permissions. An MCP client handles per-user OAuth 2.1 login flows and scoped tool permissions outside the sandbox, so connecting a remote SaaS product works without handing raw credentials to the agent. story|variant:mini|title:rust agent with.content_excerpt: A fast local inference engine for Inkling 2 Mini on Apple silicon, written in Rust and built for coding agents. It serves an OpenAI-compatible API that Codex, aider and opencode can use as they would a hosted model. It runs one model family and does not try to be general. That is what lets it do things a general engine does not: generate whole tokens in one GPU submission, keep processed prompts between requests and restarts, and copy runs of tokens the reply repeats from the conversation. The first run downloads Unsloth’s UD-Q4_K_M conversion (16.6 GB) to the Hugging Face cache, where other tools that use the Hub will find it too. rustling pull does only that, if you would rather fetch it ahead. A download that is interrupted starts again from the beginning; on an unreliable connection, hf download unsloth/Inkling-2-Mini-GGUF Inkling-2-Mini-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf can resume, and rustling finds the file it leaves. rustling chat is an assistant for the current directory, with the model in the same process: no server, no network. It can read and search files ( read , grep and glob ), asking before each call; it changes nothing and runs no commands. It is built on manifatura, an agent framework. Its own instructions are one line, cli/src/agent/system.md ; the tools' guidelines, the AGENTS.md files, the directory and the date follow it. Its instructions follow the AGENTS.md convention: ~/.config/rustling/AGENTS.md , then AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md ) in each directory from the repository root down to the current one. Sessions are kept per directory under ~/.local/share/rustling/sessions . Processed prompts are kept as serve keeps them ( --cache-gb , --cache-dir , --no-cache-dir ), so a resumed session, even after a restart, starts in seconds. The chat can use the tools of MCP servers, reached at a URL (streamable HTTP) or run on this machine (stdio), set up in ~/.config/rustling/mcp.toml . For Exa 's web search, through its hosted server: A local server is a command , with args , env and cwd ; an HTTP one takes headers and env_headers . Servers start while the model loads; one that does not start is reported and left out. A server's tools are named <server>__<tool> . Without eager they are kept out of the prompt, which matters with a small context window, and the model finds them with find_tools and runs them with run_tool . approve = true asks before each call. /mcp lists the servers and their tools. story|ver:1|title:uber evals 1m agent sk.content_excerpt: Learn more about advertising on Uber. Reach consumers as they go anywhere and get anything. A skill is a Markdown file that teaches an AI agent to do one job well, such as creating a pull request, querying a metrics store, or outlining a weekly sales presentation. Skills are one of the building blocks of Uber's software factory . Uber's shared skills marketplace grew from 1 skill in October 2025 to more than 5,000 in just one year. Thousands of people have written a skill, and agents invoked skills more than 1 million times in just one month. At enterprise scale, skill management, quality, efficiency, and distribution raise many challenges and opportunities. This post is for teams that are rolling out agents across a company. We share how to improve AI enablement and how to use agents to help. A skill is a workflow, and "the atomic unit of the enterprise is the workflow." [1] A skill packages one workflow: a runbook, a team's process, or a task an expert does by hand. It can be as short as editing a Linear® issue or as long as a full root-cause analysis. On disk, a skill is a directory. Its SKILL.md file has a name, a description, and a body of instructions. The directory can also hold scripts and reference files. An agent loads it in three stages, so thousands of skills cost only a short description each: Figure 1: A skill folder, and when an agent loads each part of it. The Agent Skills specification describes the open format in detail. We created one place for everyone to put skills, where they load easily wherever people use agents. The best place turned out to be a Git® repository, because version control already gives each skill an owner, a review, and a history. Figure 2: Skills in the agent marketplace at the end of each week over 13 months, counted from the repository's Git history. Figure 3: Recorded skill invocations per month, March to October 2026, across Claude Code™, OpenCode™, Codex™, and Uber's internal agent. The goal is to make it easy for teams to write skills while providing them with a curated set of skills by default. To enable fast but high quality development, we separate the marketplace into three tiers, and the expectations for quality and efficiency rise as a skill graduates. To graduate a skill, we run our eval system and have a set of quality and usefulness checks. Figure 4: The three tiers, what a plugin contains, and the path from pull request to release.
